s: Ealing's high point, with an Iron Age past
w: At 84 metres, Horsenden is Ealing's roof: meadow and woodland above the canal, with west London falling away from the summit. Neolithic cultivation soil and Iron Age pottery have surfaced here; keep to the paths across the protected hilltop earthwork.
_facts: Ealing Council identifies Horsenden Hill as the borough's highest point.
The summit landscape includes protected archaeological earthworks.

s: A spiral climb up west London's construction spoil
q: Northala Fields Highest Mound Northolt Greenford
w: Four grass cones rise beside the A40, shaped from spoil brought out of major London building projects. Take the gentle spiral around Northala Fields' tallest mound and the traffic drops below you; from roughly 22 metres up, the council promises a full-circle view.
_facts: Ealing Council describes four large conical mounds and a spiral route up the tallest.
The tallest mound is about 22 metres high and has a 360-degree view.

s: A Repton-shaped hill above Wembley's fields
q: Barn Hill Fryent Country Park Wembley
w: Climb out of Fryent's hay meadows into a hilltop copse and Wembley briefly feels rural. Barn Hill's surviving paths and tree clumps belong to late-18th-century landscaping associated with Humphry Repton; the reward is open country-park ground above the stadium suburbs.
_facts: Barn Hill rises within public Fryent Country Park.
The hill's landscape is associated with Humphry Repton's late-18th-century work.

s: A meridian marker on the wrong meridian
q: Pole Hill Obelisk Chingford Epping Forest
w: Forest paths climb to a skyline view and an 1824 obelisk intended to mark the Greenwich Meridian. Better measurements later put the stone slightly west of the true line. Pole Hill keeps both versions: a scientific mistake under the trees, and London on the horizon.
_facts: The City of London presents Pole Hill as a viewpoint reached through Epping Forest.
The 1824 obelisk was intended to mark the Greenwich Meridian but sits slightly west of it.

s: A suburban climb to a vanished country house
q: Gladstone Park Hilltop Dollis Hill Brent
w: A broad suburban slope climbs to the footprint of Dollis Hill House, the country retreat where William Gladstone often stayed. The damaged house was finally demolished, but its terrace and the park's high ground remain, with long views carrying the eye back across London.
_facts: Gladstone Park occupies the former Dollis Hill Estate and uses its sloping ground for views.
The park retains the footprint of demolished Dollis Hill House.

access.status: public park paths and grass routes
access.difficulty: ordinary; wet grass can be slippery

s: Woodland opens onto Croydon's stone balcony
w: Heath and woodland close around the climb, then a stone platform abruptly opens the horizon. Built in 1963 on Addington Hills' high ground, the viewpoint looks north across Croydon's roofs toward central London; the reservoir beside it remains fenced off.
_facts: Addington Hills is public heath and woodland on rising ground above Croydon.
A formal viewing platform was built in 1963 and has extensive views.

s: A gravel-capped summit with a Bronze Age barrow
w: Roots and gravel lead through protected woodland to Croham Hurst's flat high ground. Prehistoric flints have been found here and a scheduled Bronze Age round barrow survives on the summit. Follow the bridleway through the trees and leave the earthwork untouched.
_facts: Croham Hurst is a protected public woodland hill.
A scheduled round barrow occupies the summit area.

access.difficulty: roots, steep mud and shared bridleway

q: Box Hill Salomons Memorial Dorking Surrey
w: Box Hill's chalk scarp rises above the Mole to Salomons Memorial, the famous balcony over Dorking and the Weald. Earn it from the stepping stones by 275 steep steps, or take the gentler hilltop approach; either way, check wet-weather footing.
_facts: Salomons Memorial is Box Hill's best-known public viewpoint.
The National Trust documents a steep stepping-stones ascent of 275 steps and gentler hilltop access.

access.difficulty: route-dependent; steep steps or gentler hilltop access

w: At 294 metres, Leith Hill is south-east England's high point, but woodland hides the scale until the summit. An 18th-century tower lifts above the trees for another 78 steps when open; the hill itself is the prize, reached by steep, often muddy estate paths.
_facts: Leith Hill is the highest point in south-east England.
The summit tower has 78 steps and separate opening arrangements.

access.status: public estate paths; tower separately managed
access.difficulty: steep, uneven and muddy in places

s: An Iron Age fort above the Weald
w: A sandy Greensand Ridge path reaches 261 metres and the banks of an Iron Age hillfort. Holmbury Hill's southern rampart opens over the Weald, but the Hurtwood is shared ground: keep to the paths, protect the earthworks and listen for mountain bikes.
_facts: Holmbury Hill is a Greensand Ridge summit crowned by an Iron Age hillfort.
The Hurtwood is maintained for public recreation and includes shared-use paths.

access.difficulty: steep, eroded and shared with bikes

s: A hilltop church with no road to it
q: St Martha's Hill Church Chilworth Guildford
w: No road reaches St Martha's church, so every arrival ends on foot: up loose sandy paths to the solitary summit above Chilworth. The North Downs Way and the route called the Pilgrims' Way cross here, and the churchyard opens south across the Surrey hills.
_facts: St Martha's Church stands alone on the hilltop and has no road access.
The summit is crossed by the North Downs Way and the route known as the Pilgrims' Way.

access.difficulty: loose sandy slopes; no road access

s: A woodland climb that saves the view for last
w: Woodland keeps the horizon hidden until the paths reach One Tree Hill's south-facing summit, where the Weald finally spreads out below. The National Trust site lies inside the Kent Downs and is also protected as an SSSI for the uncommon life under its trees.
_facts: The National Trust manages One Tree Hill as free-access countryside with a summit view.
The site lies in the Kent Downs and is designated as an SSSI.

access.status: free countryside access dawn to dusk
access.difficulty: uneven woodland paths and steep slopes

s: A huge hillfort above prehistoric rock shelters
w: A steep wooded climb enters one of Britain's largest Iron Age hillforts, its long ramparts running through the trees above Ightham. Much older lives left traces too: Historic England records Palaeolithic rock shelters here. Walk the banks; do not wear them down.
_facts: Oldbury Hill carries one of Britain's largest Iron Age hillforts.
Historic England records Palaeolithic rock shelters within the protected monument.

access.status: National Trust countryside dawn to dusk
access.difficulty: uneven woodland paths and steep steps

s: East Sussex's open chalk high point
w: The South Downs roll up to Ditchling Beacon, East Sussex's highest point at about 248 metres. Traces of an Iron Age hillfort survive on the open chalk top; north lies the Weald, south the coast. There is no shelter from wind, rain or slick grass.
_facts: Ditchling Beacon is the highest point in East Sussex and a major South Downs summit.
The summit preserves traces of an Iron Age hillfort.

access.difficulty: exposed chalk and grass; livestock present

s: Five millennia around a wide chalk summit
w: Cissbury's chalk summit is wrapped by Sussex's largest hillfort, enclosing roughly 65 acres of a landscape used for more than 5,000 years. The uphill approach ends on broad ramparts with clear-day views toward the coast and the Isle of Wight.
_facts: Cissbury Ring is the largest hillfort in Sussex and encloses roughly 65 acres.
The National Trust describes a history extending more than 5,000 years and wide summit views.

access.difficulty: moderately steep; chalk can be slippery
